definition: Fossil (conventional) fuels are organic fuels extracted from underground deposits that formed naturally from decayed plant matter over millions of years; they are built from hydrogen-and-carbon molecules, hence the name hydrocarbons.
core_idea: Organic fuels supply the overwhelming majority of world energy, and are split into fossil fuels (ancient, extracted from the ground) versus biofuels (produced from recently grown crops).
key_points: Organic-source fuels supply more than 90% of world energy.
Fossil fuels form over millions of years from trapped, decaying plant life.
Biofuels are the same broad hydrocarbon category but sourced from recently grown crops rather than ancient underground deposits.
Burning (combusting) hydrocarbons with oxygen releases heat used to power engines or generators.
relationships: Fossil fuels and biofuels are both hydrocarbon fuels, distinguished by the age/source of the organic material rather than chemical composition.
caveats: Fossil fuel and hydrocarbon are not strict synonyms — hydrocarbon is the chemical category, while fossil fuel specifies the ancient-underground origin as opposed to biofuel.
